function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Choosing the “best” ionisation method depends on what you’re trying to analyse and the constraints of your experiment.** Below is a quick guide to help you decide which technique might suit your needs best. | Ionisation Technique | Typical Applications | Advantages | Disadvantages | When to Use | |----------------------|----------------------|------------|---------------|-------------| | **Electron Impact (EI)** | Small, volatile, thermally stable molecules (e.g., hydrocarbons, pesticides). | • Simple, robust, reproducible.
• Generates rich fragmentation patterns for library matching.
• Widely available. | • Requires high vacuum.
• Not suitable for thermally labile or high‑molecular‑weight compounds.
• Produces only singly charged ions. | • Routine GC‑MS analysis of small organics.
• When you need a well‑established fragmentation library. | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Semi‑volatile, polar, thermally labile molecules (e.g., alcohols, acids). | • Soft ionisation → less fragmentation.
• Can produce protonated or deprotonated ions.
• Compatible with GC‑MS. | • Requires a reagent gas (CH₄, NH₃, etc.).
• Lower sensitivity for some analytes.
• Still limited to GC‑MS. | • When you need to preserve molecular ions for accurate mass determination.
• When EI fragmentation is too extensive. | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Non‑polar, moderately polar, high‑MW compounds (e.g., steroids, pharmaceuticals). | • Works with LC‑MS.
• Good for moderately polar analytes.
• Handles high‑flow rates. | • Less effective for highly polar or ionic species.
• Requires a nebuliser and spray chamber. | • LC‑MS of neutral or weakly polar drugs.
• When you need a fast, “plug‑and‑play” source. | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Polar, ionic, high‑MW biomolecules (proteins, peptides, nucleic acids). | • Soft ionisation → preserves non‑covalent complexes.
• Produces multiply charged ions → extends mass range.
• Compatible with LC‑MS. | • Requires a solvent system with a suitable ionisable component.
• Susceptible to ion suppression from salts or detergents. | • Proteomics, metabolomics, large biomolecule analysis.
• When you need to detect intact macromolecules. | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Biomolecules, polymers, nanoparticles. | • Very soft ionisation → minimal fragmentation.
• Handles very high‑MW species.
• Fast acquisition. | • Requires a matrix; sample prep can be complex.
• Limited to MALDI‑TOF or MALDI‑MS/MS. | • Protein sequencing, peptide mapping, polymer analysis.
• When you need rapid screening of large biomolecules. | | **Laser Desorption Ionisation (LDI)** | Inorganic materials, nanoparticles, metal clusters. | • No matrix needed.
• Good for inorganic species. | • Limited to certain classes of analytes.
• Often requires specialized optics. | • Surface analysis, nanomaterial characterization. | | **Secondary Ion Mass Spectrometry (SIMS)** | Surface composition, thin films, microanalysis. | • Extremely high spatial resolution.
• Detects elements and isotopes. | • Requires vacuum and a primary ion beam.
• Sample damage possible. | • Materials science, semiconductor analysis. | | **Ambient Ionisation (DART, DESI, LAESI, etc.)** | Direct analysis of solids, liquids, tissues. | • Minimal sample prep.
• Rapid, real‑time analysis. | • Often lower sensitivity.
• Limited to certain matrices. | • On‑site forensic analysis, food safety, clinical diagnostics. | ### How to pick the right one 1. **Identify the analyte class** * Small, volatile organics → EI or CI (GC‑MS). * Polar, high‑MW biomolecules → ESI (LC‑MS). * Very high‑MW proteins/peptides → MALDI‑TOF. * Inorganic surfaces → SIMS or LDI. 2. **Consider the sample matrix** * Complex biological fluids → ESI (with cleanup). * Solid surfaces → SIMS or MALDI. * Ambient samples → DART or DESI. 3. **Balance sensitivity vs. fragmentation** * If you need a clear molecular ion → CI or APCI. * If you need detailed structural info → EI or ESI (with MS/MS). 4. **Check instrument availability** * Many labs have GC‑MS (EI/CI) and LC‑MS (ESI/APCI). * MALDI‑TOF is common in proteomics labs. * SIMS and ambient sources are more specialised. 5. **Think about downstream analysis** * Library matching → EI (GC‑MS). * Quantitation of large biomolecules → ESI (LC‑MS/MS). * Imaging or spatial mapping → MALDI imaging or SIMS. --- #### Quick Decision Flow ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the analyte small? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Is it volatile?│ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Use EI (GC‑MS) │ │ No → Use CI (GC‑MS) │ └───────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the analyte polar? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Is it high‑MW? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Use ESI (LC‑MS)│ │ No → Use APCI (LC‑MS)│ └───────────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the analyte inorganic? │ ├───────────────────────┤ │ Yes → Use SIMS or LDI │ │ No → Use MALDI‑TOF │ └───────────────────────┘ ``` --- ### Bottom line - **For routine GC‑MS of small organics:** EI is the gold standard. - **For polar, thermally labile GC‑MS analytes:** CI is preferable. - **For LC‑MS of polar, high‑MW biomolecules:** ESI is usually the best choice. - **For very high‑MW proteins or peptides:** MALDI‑TOF is ideal. - **For surface or material analysis:** SIMS or LDI. - **For rapid, on‑site analysis:** Ambient ionisation (DART, DESI). If you give me more details about the specific analytes, sample type, and analytical goals, I can narrow down the recommendation even further!
